key_terms.meaning: A body changes shape as it moves but keeps the same volume — a ball flattens on impact and stretches when fast, yet looks equally 'heavy' throughout.
Arranging pose, silhouette, camera angle and background so the audience reads the action instantly, with nothing important hidden.
The number of frames, and the spacing between drawings, that decides how fast and how heavy a motion looks.
A frame where the animator sets the value of a property (position, scale, colour) by hand; the software stores this value with a time stamp.
A frame generated between two keyframes by interpolating the property, so the animator does not draw it.
A tween that changes an object's properties (position, rotation, scale, alpha) while the object itself stays the same drawing.
A tween that changes the outline of a drawing from one shape into another, so the geometry itself is interpolated.
The matching of points, edges or features between the source shape and the target shape before morphing starts.
The few marked points (on an outline, a mesh or a feature such as an eye or nose) whose motion steers the whole warp.
Morphing done by visiting each pixel of the output image and asking which source pixel it came from, so every output pixel gets exactly one value.
Tracing live-action footage frame by frame to get realistic motion in a drawn animation.
A small bitmap that is moved over a background by the program instead of redrawing the whole scene each frame.
Recording a real performer's joint positions with markers or sensors and driving a 3D skeleton from that data.
Specifying the wanted position of the end of a chain (a hand, a foot) and letting the software compute the joint angles that reach it.
Animation of many small independent elements (smoke, rain, sparks) using rules for birth, velocity and death instead of keyframes.
An authoring model where the title is a stack of screens (cards or pages) and navigation moves from one card to another.
A picture stored as a grid of pixels; resolution is fixed at creation and every edit rewrites pixel values.
A layer that holds only a colour or tone change and affects the layers below it, leaving their pixels untouched.
An anchor is a point a path passes through; its two handles set the direction and length of the tangent, which fixes the curve on either side.
A smear drawn along the direction of motion, covering the distance the object travels during the shutter time, used to suggest speed.

takeaways: Squash and stretch, staging and timing are three separate checks, and a motion usually looks wrong because one of them is missing.
A keyframe stores a value; a tween is the rule that fills the frames in between, so animators set poses and the software computes motion.
Motion tweens change properties of one object, shape tweens change the outline itself, and the two fail in different ways.
Morphing needs correspondence first, then warping, then a colour cross-dissolve — skipping correspondence gives a melting, soupy result.
Forward warping leaves holes in the output, so practical morphing loops over output pixels and uses inverse warping.
2D and 3D animation are not competitors but toolkits: cels, sprites, cut-outs and rotoscoping for one look, model-rig-animate-render for another.
The authoring metaphor (card, icon, time-based) decides how a title is organised before any content is drawn, and changing it later is expensive.
Raster tools store pixels and vector tools store objects; that single choice controls resolution, file size and what kind of editing is possible.
Retouching stays reversible when every edit gets its own layer and colour changes live in adjustment layers.
A Bezier path is a short list of anchors plus handles, which is why a vector curve scales to any size without breaking.
On a timeline, easing and motion blur do most of the work of making a tween look like real motion rather than a slide.
bank_note: Long answers in this unit are judged on the pipeline or the step list — draw the stages (correspondence to warp to dissolve, model to rig to animate to render) and attach one named tool or example to each stage rather than writing general prose.

bank.q: Define squash and stretch, staging and timing, and explain how each of the three makes an animated action look believable. Give one example of a scene where ignoring each rule ruins the shot.
outline: Squash and stretch: shape changes, volume constant, example of a bouncing ball flattening on contact
Staging: clear silhouette, camera angle, contrast with background, one idea per pose
Timing: number of frames and spacing between drawings sets speed and weight
Slow-in and slow-out as a timing tool
Failure examples: rigid ball looks like stone, cluttered pose unreadable, evenly spaced frames look mechanical

bank.q: Define keyframe, in-between and tween. Explain how the software computes the in-between values for position, scale and colour, and state what an ease curve does to that computation.
outline: Keyframe = frame with an author-set value and a time stamp
Tween = interpolation rule between two keyframes
In-between = generated frame value; linear interpolation formula for a property
Separate interpolation per property (position, scale, rotation, alpha)
Easing = non-linear time remapping, slow-in slow-out

bank.q: Explain the three authoring metaphors — card or page based, icon or object based, and time based — with the kind of title each suits and one example tool for each.
outline: Card/page: stack of screens, navigation by links, suits kiosks, CBT and presentations
Icon/object: flow chart of icons with the event and result of each, suits training simulations and branching logic
Time based: timeline of layers and keyframes, suits animation and video, suits synchronising sound to picture
Cross-platform authoring tools and why a common runtime matters
How the metaphor fixes the author's workflow before content is created

bank.q: Distinguish painting tools from drawing tools in terms of what they store, then compare raster and vector images on resolution, editing, file size and scaling.
outline: Painting stores a pixel grid; drawing stores objects and attributes
Raster: fixed resolution, pixel-level editing, size grows with resolution, degrades on scaling
Vector: resolution independent, object-level editing, compact files, needs rasterising for output
When each is chosen: photo retouching vs logos, type, diagrams

bank.q: Describe the morphing of one face image into another as a sequence of steps. Cover correspondence, control points or mesh, warping, colour cross-dissolve, and explain why inverse warping is used in practice.
outline: Choose control points or build a mesh on both images, with guaranteed correspondence
Warp both toward an intermediate geometry, gradually over the frame sequence
Interpolate colours, cross-dissolve weight rising from 0 to 1
Forward warping leaves holes and overlaps; inverse warping samples the source at the mapped output pixel
Interpolation of control point positions, bilinear or spline warping
Artifacts: ghosting, tearing, need for good correspondence

bank.q: You must draw a smooth logo curve with the pen tool. Explain placing an anchor, dragging out handles to set the tangent, adding further anchors, closing the path, and converting the path to a filled selection. State what happens to the curve when a handle is lengthened.
outline: Anchor point = point on the path; handles = tangent direction and length
Click places a corner point, click-drag places a smooth point
Segment shape controlled by both neighbouring handles
Closing the path and filling it
Converting path to selection and back
Longer handle = flatter, wider curve; rotating handle bends the segment

bank.q: Explain how to build a timeline animation of a symbol moving across the stage: keyframes, motion tween, path, easing, motion blur, and testing the movie. Mention nesting and swapping the tween target.
outline: Convert object to symbol, place start keyframe and end keyframe
Create motion tween; timeline interpolates position, scale, rotation, alpha
Guide path or motion path for a curved route
Easing to slow in and slow out
Motion blur spanning the shutter interval
Nested animation inside a symbol; swapping the tween target
Testing the movie, checking frame rate and playback

bank.q: Describe a non-destructive photo retouching workflow: background copy, separate layers per correction, adjustment layers for tone and colour, filters applied to duplicate layers, masks, and the final save in an editable and a delivery format.
outline: Duplicate background so the original survives
One layer per retouch: healing, clone, dodge and burn
Adjustment layers for levels, curves, hue and saturation, affecting all layers below
Layer masks to limit where an edit applies
Smart filters or filters on duplicates so the effect can be changed or removed
Layer order, opacity and blending mode
Save layered master plus flattened delivery copy

bank.q: A short 3D film needs a character walk cycle, a rain storm and a crowd. Explain the model-rig-animate-render pipeline and choose a technique for each of the three requirements, justifying the choice.
outline: Pipeline: modelling, texturing, rigging, animation, lighting, rendering
Rig: skeleton, joints, forward kinematics by joint angles, inverse kinematics by target position
Walk cycle: keyframe or motion capture; IK for feet planted on the ground
Rain: particle system with birth rate, velocity, gravity, lifetime
Crowd: instancing plus procedural or rule-based motion rather than hand keyframing
Render pass, frame rate and file output

bank.q: Compare a shape tween with a morph based on correspondence and warping. For a face-to-face transformation, analyse which gives better control, which artifacts each produces, and how to reduce them.
outline: Shape tween interpolates outlines directly with no user control over which part goes where
Morph adds explicit correspondence and control points, so eyes map to eyes
Shape tween artifacts: unwanted twisting, self-intersection, lost features
Morph artifacts: ghosting, stretching, holes from forward warping
Fixes: add control points, split into regions, use inverse warping, adjust dissolve timing
Cost: morph needs more setup work and manual correspondence

bank.q: A studio must produce a weekly 2D cartoon on a small budget. Evaluate frame-by-frame, cut-out and rotoscoping approaches on cost, production time, motion quality and reusability, and recommend one with reasons.
outline: Frame-by-frame: full control and fluid motion, highest drawing cost per second
Cut-out: build puppet once, reuse by moving parts, cheap and fast, limited to planar motion, needs good rigging
Rotoscoping: realistic motion, needs footage and tracing time per frame, suits realism
Reusability of assets, library of poses
Hybrid approach: cut-out for body, frame-by-frame for key action
Justified recommendation with the trade-off stated

bank.q: Choose an authoring metaphor for an interactive simulation that teaches safe wiring practice in a training centre, with scoring, branching and voice narration. Justify the choice and explain how objects, events and the timeline are used.
outline: Icon or object-based flow suits branching logic and simulation states
Cards or pages used for the introduction and results screens
Timeline used for the animated demonstration sequences and synchronising narration
Object definition: properties, events handled, response to user action
Cross-platform authoring and delivery to lab machines
Testing, feedback and scoring loop

bank.q: Evaluate destructive editing against layers and adjustment layers in an image editing tool. Discuss reversibility, quality loss on repeated saves, file size, review workflow and when destructive editing is acceptable.
outline: Destructive edits overwrite pixels; each save can lose data
Repeated compression and tone edits degrade the image
Layers and adjustment layers keep the original pixels and allow later change
Masks make corrections local rather than global
Cost: larger layered files, slower processing, need for a flattened delivery copy
Acceptable cases: final small exports, batch processing, work that will never be revisited

bank.q: Analyse how frame spacing, easing and motion blur together create the sense of speed and weight in a timeline animation, and discuss the cost of motion blur in render time and how much is enough.
outline: Frame spacing sets apparent speed and, with spacing changes, acceleration
Slow-in and slow-out mimic real acceleration under gravity
Fewer frames on a fast move plus stretch reads as speed
Motion blur = displacement over shutter interval, direction follows the velocity vector
More blur samples means smoother smear but linear cost per frame
Blur plus easing reads as weight; too much blur reads as mush

glossary.def: Producing the illusion of motion by showing a sequence of slightly different still images fast enough for the eye to blend them.
The number of frames shown per second; film commonly 24, television 25 or 30, measured in frames per second (fps).
The tendency of the eye and brain to hold an image briefly, which lets separate frames appear as continuous motion.
A frame where the animator fixes the value of a property by hand.
Computing intermediate values between two known values, which is how tweening fills in-between frames.
A generated set of frames between two keyframes, produced by interpolating one or more properties.
Making the interpolation speed up or slow down instead of running at constant rate, so motion starts and stops naturally.
Showing faint copies of neighbouring frames under the current one so the animator can judge the spacing of a motion.
Smoothly turning one image or shape into another by warping geometry and blending colour over time.
Moving pixel positions according to a mapping, so a shape deforms without being redrawn.
Warping controlled by a grid of control points laid over the image, each point dragged to a new position.
Blending two images by raising the opacity of one while lowering the other, used at the end of a morph.
Drawing or painting characters on transparent sheets laid over a painted background, so the background is not redrawn each frame.
Building a character from separate pieces and moving the pieces to animate, instead of drawing new frames.
Building the skeleton and controls that let an animator pose a 3D model.
Setting each joint angle in a chain by hand and computing where the end of the chain lands; the reverse problem is inverse kinematics.
Motion produced by rules or formulas rather than keyframes, such as physics-driven or noise-driven movement.
Turning the scene or timeline into final output pixels, with lighting, shading and effects applied.
Software used to assemble text, graphics, sound, video and interactivity into a finished interactive title.
An authoring model where the title is a flow chart of icons, each carrying an event and a resulting action.
An authoring model where content sits on layers along a timeline, giving frame-level control of timing.
Softening the edges of drawn shapes by blending boundary pixels with the background, reducing jagged stair-steps.
A curve defined by two end anchors and handles that set the tangent direction and strength at each anchor.
A grayscale channel attached to a layer that hides or reveals parts of it without deleting pixels.
The fraction of a frame time during which the virtual camera is open, which sets how long a motion-blur smear becomes.
